title: Math: Reverse Integer (Overflow and Negative Modulo)
oneLiner: Reverse a 32-bit integer's digits, returning 0 if the result doesn't fit: the lesson where C# and Python disagree about both % and overflow.
keyTakeaway: Pop digits with x % 10 and push them with result * 10 + digit, checking BEFORE the multiply that result can't pass int.MaxValue / 10. In C#, % keeps the sign of x, so negatives just work and an unchecked overflow wraps silently. In Python, % follows the divisor's sign and ints never overflow, so handle the sign yourself and compare against the 32-bit limits explicitly.
explanation:
Given a signed 32-bit integer x, return x with its digits reversed. If the reversed value is outside the 32-bit signed range, -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, return 0. Pretend the environment can't store 64-bit integers, so the check has to happen without a bigger type. 123 becomes 321, -123 becomes -321, 120 becomes 21, and 1,534,236,469 becomes 0 (9,646,324,351 is too big).

The digit loop: digit = x % 10 takes the last digit, x /= 10 drops it, and result = result * 10 + digit pushes it onto the end of the answer. The overflow guard goes right before the push: if result > int.MaxValue / 10 (214,748,364), multiplying by 10 is already too big. If result equals 214,748,364 exactly, the push only fits if digit <= 7 (the last digit of 2,147,483,647). The negative side is the mirror image with int.MinValue / 10 and -8.

C#: integer division truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the left operand, so -123 % 10 is -3 and -123 / 10 is -12. The same loop handles negative x with no special case. Without the guard, result * 10 wraps round silently (C# arithmetic is unchecked by default) and you return garbage instead of 0. Wrapping the expression in checked(...) would throw an OverflowException instead, which also works if you catch it.

Python: // rounds DOWN and % takes the sign of the right operand, so -123 % 10 is 7 and -123 // 10 is -13. Running the C# loop on a negative number gives nonsense. Take the sign first, reverse abs(x), then put the sign back. And since Python ints never overflow, nothing will stop you at 2^31: compare against 2**31 - 1 and -2**31 yourself.

The visualization reverses -123, with the C# view of % and /.

visualizationSteps.message: x = -123. In C#, x % 10 keeps x's sign and x / 10 truncates toward zero, so the loop works for negatives unchanged. The cells are the digits popped so far.
-123 % 10 = -3 and -123 / 10 = -12. Guard: |result| is far below 214,748,364, so result * 10 + -3 = -3 is safe.
-12 % 10 = -2 and -12 / 10 = -1. Guard: |result| is far below 214,748,364, so result * 10 + -2 = -32 is safe.
-1 % 10 = -1 and -1 / 10 = 0. Guard: |result| is far below 214,748,364, so result * 10 + -1 = -321 is safe.
x is 0: answer -321. In Python, -123 % 10 is 7 and -123 // 10 is -13, so the same loop would go wrong there: reverse abs(x) and restore the sign.

recognitionSignals: "Assume a 32-bit environment" or "return 0 if the result overflows".
Building a number digit by digit with result * 10 + digit (also atoi, string to integer).
Negative inputs combined with % or integer division.
gotchas: Check for overflow BEFORE result * 10, not after: after the multiply the damage is done (C# wraps, the comparison is meaningless).
Python's % and // round toward negative infinity: -123 % 10 is 7, not -3. Strip the sign first.
abs(int.MinValue) overflows in C# (Math.Abs throws OverflowException). The C# loop never needs abs because % keeps the sign.
confusableWith: Palindrome Number reverses digits the same way (or only half of them) but compares instead of returning.
String to Integer (atoi) has the identical result * 10 + digit overflow guard, with parsing on top.

complexity.note: One round per decimal digit, at most 10 for a 32-bit int, with two variables.

referenceSolutions.python:
def reverse(x):
    # Python's % and // round toward negative infinity (-123 % 10 == 7), so strip the sign first.
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    x = abs(x)
    result = 0
    while x:
        x, digit = divmod(x, 10)
        result = result * 10 + digit
    result *= sign
    # Python ints never overflow, so the 32-bit limits have to be checked by hand.
    if result < -2**31 or result > 2**31 - 1:
        return 0
    return result
